analytic.title: Using Harmonic Task-Sets to Increase the Schedulable Utilization of Cache-based Preemptive Real-Time Systems*

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Cache memories have been traditionally precluded in real-time systems because of their unpredictable behavior. The needs of better performance have motivated the development of tools to obtain tighter bounds on the worst-case execution time (WCET) of cached programs. However, they do not allow preemption, because from the point of view of program analysis, the number of preemptions is unknown. To face this problem, the cacherelated preemption cost can be considered in the schedulability analysis, or annulled by the use of private cache partitions. Regarding the first approach, in a previous paper we described how to incorporate the effect of the cache to the Response Time schedulability Analysis (RTA). RTA is an efficient analysis for preemptive fixedpriority schedulers. In this paper, we have improved such a technique by taking into account the harmonic relations amongst task frequencies. The resulting analysis is applied to sample task-sets to illustrate the potential gains in terms of schedulable utilization, particularly for highly demanding task-sets.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Cache memories are becoming inevitable as a mean to provide the memory bandwidth requested by contemporary processors. For example, for the DEC Alpha 21064 running at 200 Mhz, one cache miss penalty is equivalent to the execution of 100 instructions [21].

Some tools have been developed to calculate the worst-case execution time (WCET) of tasks taking into account the cache speed-up [1][14] [16]. These tools assume continuity for the code execution, because from the point of view of program analysis, the number of preemptions is unknown. This limitation restricts the application of such tools to non preemptive scheduling policies like cyclic executives or co-operative scheduling.

However, this limitation is an inconvenience, since preemptive schedulers (in particular fixed-priority) are very flexible [ 181, and their theory has been extensively extended to meet practical requirements [6].

Two solutions can be used to make caches suitable for preemptive real-time systems, either using partitioning, or modelling the extrinsic (inter-task) cache behavior to incorporate the cache-related preemption delays in the schedulability analysis.

Regarding the latter approach, in a previous paper [9] we presented CRTA (Cached Response Time schedulability Analysis) which is a derivation of RTA. The estimation of the extrinsic cache behavior (or interference) is divided in the assessment of the worst-case number of preemptions that a given task may suffer, and the worstcase cache-related delay that a preemption may inflict. Even though the results obtained by CRTA were promising, the model can be further refined. In this paper, we provide a better estimation of the number of preemptions.

In real-time applications, many tasks exhibit harmonic frequencies (see Table I). This characteristic can be exploited to improve the estimated number of preemptions. On the other hand, the new model will be sensitive to tasks phasings. Therefore, other issues, like synchronization, may now affect the worst-case estimation. The previous work is briefly reviewed in section 2. We summarize in section 3 the exact schedulability analysis RTA, which form the basis of the cached extension CRTA (section 4). Section 5 presents a refinement of CRTA based on the harmonic frequencies of tasks. The resulting analysis is compared to CRTA in section 6. Finally the conclusions are stated in section 7.

div.head: Scope and limitations
div.p: This work is focused on uniprocessor systems. However, it is valid for multiprocessor/distributed systems, where tasks are allocated statically to processors.

For simplicity, we have considered only one-level instruction caches (of any organization). But the theory can be easily extended to levelled schemes or data caches. Besides, since the cache-related preemption delay is proportional to cache size, one-level medium-size caches are usually the best choice.

This work is focused on fixed-priority preemptive realtime systems. The technique proposed is aimed at improving the schedulable utilization (the utilization bound guaranteed by a given analysis), not the performance.

We are only concerned with the extrinsic (inter-task) behavior of the cache. Thus we will concentrate on aspects of the extrinsic behavior while assuming implicitly that the intrinsic behavior has already been taken into account, for example when calculating the WCET of tasks for the evaluation of the analysis in section 6.

div.head: Previous work
div.p: The first technique dealing with extrinsic cache behavior is cache partitioning. Cache partitioning [13] [24] is aimed at improving the cache predictability by annulling the extrinsic interference by providing each task with a private cache partition.

Another approach for dealing the problem, started with CRMA (Cached Rate Monotonic Analysis) introduced by Basumallick and Nilsen in [4]. CRMA takes into account the extrinsic cache interference in the utilization based RMA test [15]. The limitations of this method stem from the pessimistic utilization bound given by RMA [22]. A comparison of this technique and cache partitioning was presented in [ 81.

To alleviate this problem, we introduced [9] and evaluated [lo] the CRTA technique. CRTA (Cached Response Time Analysis) is the cached version of the exact schedulability test RTA for fixed priority preemptive real-time systems. We will review this work in the next two sections as a background material for section 5 , the main contribution of this paper. A comparison of CRTA to both partitioning and CRMA was given in [lo].
This paper is a continuity of the work done in [8][9] and [lo].

div.head: Exact schedulability analysis
div.p: The unnecessary pessimistic utilization bound given by the utilization based RM analysis motivated the development of exact (sufficient and necessary) tests. We will concentrate on the Response Time Analysis (RTA) [2][11][12]. The computational model assumes a fixed priority task-set. Non-periodic tasks are allowed provided that a minimum inter-arrival time can be guaranteed. The test is independent of the priority assignment policy used, but priorities must be fixed and unique (although they can be eventually raised due to inheritance protocols to resource control).

The analysis calculates the worst-case response time for each task, and compares it to the allowed deadline. The worst-case response time is produced when all the tasks are released at the same time point (critical instant), and a recursive approach is used to assess it. The approach tries to allocate in a time window w, the task zi computation time C,, the task's blocking time B, and the interference produced by the execution of higher priority tasks. The blocking time is the maximum time that the task may be delayed by lower priority tasks due to resource contention. The process is recursive because at every step the interference is added to the current window w,", so resulting in a longer time window w,"" that might include greater interference in the next step. div.head: Incorporating the extrinsic cache interference to the analysis
div.p: The extrinsic cache interference suffered by each task is an additional interference to be considered in the recursive relation. The problem can be divided: how many times the interference is accounted, and how long is its time penalty.
To address the first problem, the following property gives the key to bound this interference [9]:
"The maximum number of preemptions suffered by a given task is bounded by the number of releases of higher priority task in its response time window ".

The second problem is to assess the cache interference penalty associated with every preemption (cache-related preemption delay). Even though there are several models, according to the preemption model (where only the preempting tasks are known) the extrinsic interference can be considered as:

In this case, the term Ci is the WCET taking into account the cache speed-up, estimated by the use of an appropriate tool and assuming that the code is executed stream-line.

div.head: Considering harmonic frequencies
div.p: In this section we show how the number of estimated preemptions can be greatly reduced when the harmonic relation amongst task periods is taken into consideration. We will start with a simple model to derive the new recurrence relation for schedulability analysis. A sample taskset is used to illustrate the rationale behind the model. Subsequently, the synchronization problems are discussed to build a more general framework.

div.head: Preemption model
div.p: The basic CRTA analysis outlined in section 4 accounts one preemption for each higher priority task that is released into the response time window of the task under analysis. This can be envisioned as that each task is executed in isolation preempting the task of interest. However, when task periods are harmonic, tasks are released at the same time point. div.p: Let us focus on the calculation of the response time for task 4. In particular, we are interested in the number of preemptions suffered by such a task. Since the period of task 2 is a multiple of the period of task 1 (task 1 frequency is a harmonic of task 2 frequency), the release of task 2 will always coincide with one release of task 1. Since task 1 has a higher priority, it will be dispatched first. Once this task completes execution, task 2 is started. Notice that the harmonic relation between these task frequencies means that task 2 will be always executed jointly with task 1 (for any instance). div.head: Synchronization problems
div.p: The model previously discussed is sensitive to the tasks phasings, as tasks with harmonic frequencies are assumed to execute together. However, some factors may vary the normal execution of tasks. For instance, when resources are used, tasks need to synchronize in order to acquire them. In particular, priority inheritance protocols (such as CSP) require task priorities to be raised, which may change the normal execution phasing of tasks.

CSP belongs to a class of resource control techniques which are predictable, perform blocking and change priorities [3]. It is a refinement of the PCP (Priority Ceiling Protocol) [23] which reduces the number of context switches. The rules for PCP can be summarised as follows: 1. A priority ceiling is assigned to each resource equal to the priority of the maximum priority task that may acquire it. 2. A resource is granted if the requested task has a priority strictly greater than the ceilings of all currently acquired resources. If the task cannot satisfy this condition, such a task becomes blocked upon the resource. 3. A task may inherit the priority of a higher priority task, if the latter becomes blocked upon the resource held by the former. The blocking task restores its priority once the execution on the critical section has completed. CSP is a refinement of PCP changing the third condition. Under CSP, the priority of a task is automatically raised (to the resource priority ceiling) when the resource is acquired. This way, a higher priority task that may potentially use the same resource, will be precluded from execution, until the resource is released. Since the higher priority task does not even start execution, it will not be stopped upon the request of the resource.

The remainder of this section will assess a bound for the maximum number of additional preemptions that CSP may inflict. We will study several cases of priority inheritance, and how it might affect the schedule of the task under interest. The schedulability analysis checks the response time for each task. We will focus on the calculation of the response time for a particular task, and the findings can be extended to other tasks, therefore being valid for the entire analysis of the task-set.

div.head: Lower priority tasks
div.p: Let us consider the example depicted in Figure 2, which corresponds to the task-set specified in Table 11. In this example, we are interested solely in the response time for task 4. Since task 1 and task 2 have harmonic fre- quencies, the execution of task 2 always follows the execution of task 1. This precludes task 4 from being preempted by task 2. Now, let consider that task 5 and task 2 shares a resource. The priority ceiling of such a resource will be equal to the priority of task 2. Hence, task 5 will raise its priority to that level if the resource is granted.

This may delay task 2 with respect to task 1. However, it cannot cause an additional preemption to task 4, since task 4 is also delayed. As can be seen, task 4 suffers an additional preemption by the tasks 1 and 2 due to the delay. However, this preemption is a consequence of a greater response time due to the blocking time, and hence it is implicitly considered in the analysis (by the term B,) while calculating recursively the response time.
In fact, task 5 cannot produce preemption to task 4 since the former is started at its real priority, which is lower than the one for task 4.

div.head: Higher priority tasks
div.p: If the priority of a higher priority task is raised due to resource control, it cannot affect the schedule of the task of interest since those tasks have higher priorities anyway.

div.p: This is the only case that may cause problems. As can be seen in Figure 3, if task 4 (which is the task for which the response time has to be calculated) increases its priority, it may delay the execution of task 2 with respect to task 1, resulting in an additional preemption. As can be seen in the proposed example, task 2 preempts task 4 in isolation once the latter has released the resource.

div.head: Summarising the synchronization effect
div.p: From the above discussions, we conclude that a task may experience at most one additional preemption for each time it uses a resource with a ceiling higher than its priority (because it is also used by a higher priority task). This observation leads to a new recurrence relation to calculate the response time for tasks (Equation 5).

This expression can be further improved if we consider, for each priority above T,, exactly which resources are shared with T,, and which preemptions are saved. However, some simulations have shown that the above equation obtains good results even for complex task-sets (30 tasks with 60 resources).

div.head: Evaluation of HCRTA
div.p: An evaluation is performed to compare the proposed approach (HCRTA) to the previous (CRTA) in terms of the maximum useful utilization that can be guaranteed (schedulable utilization). Both analyses are used to check schedulability of randomly generated sample task-sets. In order to study the influence of some important factors (like frequency and number of tasks), the parameters of the task-set are generated based on them. One of the tasks is set to the maximum frequency (minimum period), and the remainder task's periods are multiple of it. This allows the use of Equation 4. For simplicity, no shared resources are considered.

It is also necessary to have a hardware model to establish the cache-related preemption delay (refill the entire cache), and the fraction of time a task wastes on cache misses (intrinsic cache behavior). We have adopted here the same hardware model explained in previous work of the authors [8]. In this particular case, the memory read time is fixed to 40 nS, the cache size is varied from 6 to 60 Kb, and the processor power is 50 MIPS.

For a given system configuration, the overall utilization is decreased until the test is passed. For the analysis, the extrinsic cache interference is accounted in the recurrence equation, while the computation time includes the delays introduced by the intrinsic cache behavior. However, the graphs only depict the useful schedulable utilization (it does not include neither intrinsic nor extrinsic delays).

Finally, the schedulable utilization obtained for each method is scaled to isolate the cache overhead to the natural loss of utilization due to the task-set configuration. For example, a non fully harmonic task-set is not likely to reach 100% utilization due to the frequency and computation time relation among tasks. The scale ratio is calculated from the maximum schedulable utilization when neither intrinsic nor extrinsic cache interference have been taken into account.

div.head: Results of the evaluation
div.p: The plotted results are the average schedulable utilization for a set of 100 sample task-sets. The size of the set of samples produces 95% confidence intervals for the mean that validates the correctness of the results.

In addition to compare HCRTA and CRTA, we have also depicted the case when no cache is considered (RTA plane) in Figure 7, to have a view of the potential benefits of the cached schemes. Three factors are studied: cache size (X-axis), number of tasks (Y-axis) and frequency (varied across the first three figures).

From the figures 5 to 8 it can be concluded that the proposed analysis (Harmonic CRTA or HCRTA) outperforms CRTA. The difference between them can be seen in Figure 8, where it is shown that the increase of performance of HCRTA over CRTA can be over 40% of schedulable utilization. This figure also reveals that the increase is almost constant for different system frequencies (being slightly better for 500 Hz, and worse for 1000 Hz). However, it is approximately linearly dependent of the number of tasks and cache size. It can be roughly explained as follows: for larger caches, the cache-related preemption delay is longer, and while the difference between the preemptions predicted by HCRTA and CRTA remains constant, the former will increase the benefits. The rationale behind the number of tasks will be explained in the next paragraph. The parallel baselines depicted in Figure 5 and Figure 6 respect to the Y-axis reveal that HCRTA performs almost constantly for different number of tasks, while CRTA is very influenced by this factor. This is because even though a larger number of tasks will produce more preemptions, a larger proportion of them are likely to have harmonic relationships with the one with the highest frequency.

As it was previously presented in [lo] (and it can also be seen in Figure 7), CRTA may reach even a 4x performance ratio over not using the cache improvements at all. In addition, even for larger task-sets and/or high frequencies, the HCRTA can take advantage of the use of caches.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: It has been shown that it is possible to further increase the schedulable utilization provided by CRTA by taking into account some harmonic relations among task frequencies. In Real-Time applications, there is trade-off between running tasks at the required frequency, or running them more often to obtain harmonic frequencies.

The technique proposed in this paper improves CRTA particularly for high demanding task-sets (high frequencies and many tasks). Therefore, this technique can be used when CRTA is not effective. In conclusion, the contributions presented has extended the applicability domain of cache memories in preemptive real-time systems.
Finally, the evaluation results presented may be used as design guidelines in the application of such a scheme.
